sentences.text: The Bois de Herbeuval ran seven minutes behind the rest of Belgium and had done since 1944, and Sidonie grew up assuming this was normal, in the way that children assume whatever is around them.
It is not a figure of speech and it is not about clocks.
There is no clock in that wood.
What there is is a toad, under the third stone up from the ford, and everything in that wood takes its time from him.
Sidonie has looked at him perhaps thirty times in her life and has never once found him interesting to look at.
He is a common toad, *Bufo bufo*, of the size and colour and general demeanour of every other common toad in the Ardennes.

If you turned that stone over on a wet evening you would think nothing of him whatsoever, and every visiting biologist who has ever been shown him has thought nothing of him, and two of them have said so out loud in a way that Sidonie's grandfather never entirely forgave.

She had it explained to her at about six by her grandfather, who was the forester there for thirty-one years, and who explained it the way he explained the difference between beech and hornbeam — patiently, once, on the assumption that she would remember.
Dusk in a wood is not a time.
It is an event.
The birds go down in an order — blackbird, then robin, then wren — and the order is fixed and the intervals are fixed and every wood in Europe does it.
The deer come out.
The bats come off the roof of the old sawmill.
The moths that come to the lime trees come, and they come within about ninety seconds of each other, every night, all summer.
All of that is triggered by light, in the books.
And the books are right, and Sidonie would like that on the record before anything else, because she has a diploma and she is not going to spend it on this.
Light level drops below a threshold; the blackbird's eye reports it; the blackbird goes.
It has been measured a thousand times in a thousand woods and there is no mystery in it at all.
In the Bois de Herbeuval it is triggered by him.
You can watch it happen if you know where to stand.

There is a moment — a small dry sound, not a croak, more like a stone dropped in leaf litter — and about four seconds after it the blackbird goes, and then the whole thing unwinds down the valley in order, and the wood puts itself to bed.
The four seconds is the part that undoes people.
Sound travels.
If the blackbird is two hundred metres up the valley it should hear the sound about six-tenths of a second after it is made, and if it is four hundred metres away it should be later still.
It is not.

Sidonie's grandfather put two people with two watches at two distances on eleven separate evenings in the summer of 1978 and the delay was four seconds at both, and he did it again in 1981 with three people because he did not believe himself the first time.
Sidonie's grandfather had timed it against a wristwatch on and off for thirty years and had it written in the back of a notebook, and the notebook is where the seven minutes comes from.
